claims.text: The material under study is equiatomic, as-solidified FeNiCrMn.
Dynamic mechanical behavior across temperature and strain-rate regimes is governed primarily by a temperature-dependent transition in dislocation mobility.
At low temperatures and high strain rates, insufficient thermal activation enhances dislocation drag and pile-up.
Enhanced dislocation drag and pile-up at low temperatures and high strain rates produce significant strain hardening.
At higher temperatures and lower strain rates, thermal activation facilitates dislocation glide.
Thermally facilitated dislocation glide reduces strain-rate sensitivity.
The evolution of dislocation density, pile-ups, and arrangement mediates the dynamic mechanical response.
Dislocation mobility is governed by thermally activated overcoming of atomic-scale obstacles.
Limited thermal energy at low temperature and high strain rate increases yield strength through dislocation drag and pile-up.
Low temperatures and high strain rates will produce a pronounced nonlinear increase in yield strength.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate deformation will produce significant dislocation pile-ups and distinct dislocation substructures observable by TEM.
At higher temperatures and moderate strain rates, yield strength will have a less steep dependence on strain rate.
At higher temperatures and moderate strain rates, dislocations will be distributed more uniformly.
The proposed study spans 77–500 K and strain rates of approximately 10^-4–10^3 s^-1.
Room-temperature testing near 300 K under quasi-static loading serves as the experimental baseline.
The hypothesis may cease to apply if deformation mechanisms such as twinning become dominant.
